books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, A. Religious and Spiritual Movements in Antebellum America

stimulus.text: In August 1801, the Presbyterian minister Barton W. Stone hosted a communion service at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, that became the largest camp meeting of the Great Revival in the West. For six days, from August 6 to 12, crowds estimated at ten to twenty thousand people gathered on the grounds, far more than the log meetinghouse, which seated about four hundred, could hold. Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers all preached, and hundreds took communion at tables set up in the woods.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Disciples of Christ Historical Society account of the Cane Ridge Revival and the National Park Service nomination for Cane Ridge: August 6-12, 1801; Barton W. Stone; estimates of ten to twenty thousand; meetinghouse capacity about four hundred; Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the Disciples Historical Society / NPS account of Cane Ridge (1801)
stem: Cane Ridge is best understood as the starting point for which of the following developments?

options.text: The founding of the Mormon church in upstate New York in 1830
options.misconception: Cane Ridge was a famous revival and Mormonism was a famous new sect, so one can look like the start of the other.

options.text: The camp-meeting pattern of outdoor, multi-day revivals that spread across the nation
The building of the Erie Canal, which carried revival preachers westward
options.misconception: The canal carried people west, so a Kentucky revival can look like a product of the canal.

options.text: The disestablishment of state-supported churches in New England
options.misconception: Church and state separated then, so a big revival can look like part of that legal change.

rationales.A: Mormonism grew from the burned-over district of New York in 1830, three decades after Cane Ridge and hundreds of miles away. Cane Ridge did not found it.
rationales.B: Cane Ridge set the pattern: days outdoors, many preachers, huge crowds, and communion in the woods. Camp meetings then spread everywhere.
rationales.C: The Erie Canal opened in 1825, twenty-four years after Cane Ridge, and it runs through New York, not Kentucky. The canal cannot explain a Kentucky meeting.
rationales.D: Disestablishment was a legal change in New England, finished in Massachusetts in 1833. Cane Ridge was a Kentucky revival, not a law about church support.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what Cane Ridge did first at this scale: six days outdoors, thousands of people, many preachers.
2. Ask what came after: camp meetings across the frontier and then the nation, using the same form.
3. Name its place: a starting point, the meeting that showed the pattern worked.
Background: Cane Ridge became the standard against which American revivals were measured for most of the nineteenth century.
Remember: a starting point is not a cause of everything after it, but it is the pattern everyone copies.
